I am informed that when a bill is read a first time the press have a right to look at it and to take from it such extracts as they think desirable by applying to the clerk's office. speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question which the hon. gentleman has asked is not difficult to answer. Timber Distributors, a British firm, the members of which have been indicated previously in discussions of this house, has entered into an agreement at Paris with the Soviet Union of Russia for a supply of timber to Great Britain.
The terms of the contract are not known to the government, but during all the period of time that has elapsed, when a new contract between Timber Distributors and the Russian

Railway Commission
authorities has been in contemplation the Canadian government has been in close touch with the situation and has urged upon the authorities the necessity of such a clause being eliminated from any contract that might be made.
I think there is much misapprehension with respect to some facts in connection with these contracts. These contracts do not arise out of the Ottawa agreement, but in the Ottawa agreement there was provision that any contracts that might be made between British importers and the Soviet Union that prejudicially affected the preference granted Canadian or other empire products in the British market would be dealt with in the manner indicated in that clause.
Last year representations were made to the government of Great Britain in consequence of a proposed contract between Timber Distributors and the Russian authorities for the purchase of quantities of timber. The quantity was limited by the quota and the fall clause, so called, disappeared. The new contract has not yet reached the point where it is possible to make representations to the government, but they have been made in the meantime, anticipating the possibility of the contract, in the strongest possible terms.
The task has become more difficult for reasons which I need not refer to at this time other than to say that an effort has been made, apparently, to convey the impression that Canadians attach little value to these provisions or to the preference itself, and that has somewhat increased the difficulty of dealing with it from the government standpoint. But every possible step is being taken by representations made by the high commissioner, at the instance of this government, to the British government. When the matter reaches the president of the board of trade more formal representations will be made.
It has been suggested by one of my colleagues that the provision of the clause in the Ottawa agreement dealing with contracts that prejudicially affected the operation of the preference was applicable to all countries and not to any one country, as my statement might possibly imply.

When the Prime Minister speaks
of the government not having information with respect to the proposed import of Russian timber, or at any rate with respect to an arrangement, does he mean the British government or the Canadian government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Neither the British nor
the Canadian government is concerned in the first instance with a contract, made by a private company known as Timber Distributors, with the Russian authorities. After the contract is made, if it is believed that that contract contravenes in any way the provisions of the section of the Ottawa agreement dealing with the matter to which I have referred, it is competent for the Canadian government to make representations to the British government, which has taken power from parliament to deal with the matter, and then action is taken in accordance with the provisions of the British statute.

Pensions for the Blind

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO EXTEND BENEFITS OF OLD AGE PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE.
speechtext: I wish to say a few words in support of this resolution, because I think the hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. Cotnam) is to be commended for bringing the matter to the attention of the house. For quite a number of years now the various organizations that have made the welfare of the blind a part of their work have been advocating adequate provision in some way for the blind. Personally I should like to see adequate provision made not only for those blind who are over forty years of age but even for those who have not reached that age, if it were necessary. I am not finding fault with the mover of the resolution for putting it in the form in which he did; in fact, I believe it was necessary to put it in that form in order to get it a hearing in the house. I simply wish to add my word of approval.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO EXTEND BENEFITS OF OLD AGE PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE.
speechtext: I most heartily endorse this resolution and I think the people throughout Canada will do the same. I know quite well that not only in this house but throughout the dominion it will receive sympathetic consideration. In my long professional career I have come in contact on many occasions with blind people both young and old, and I have been afflicted nearer home than perhaps most hon. gentlemen have been. One thing has always struck me in regard to the blind, something that I have observed more among them than among those suffering from any other affliction, and that is their great earnestness and their willingness to work. We see the blind wandering along the streets, stick in hand, with no other help than their other senses, which no doubt do become more acute, finding their way about, and taking up lessons in music and in other occupations. They are always willing to help themselves. Since its introduction Braille has been of great benefit to the blind. I know of many instances where they both read and write in Braille, and now there are magazines in that system, and they have the benefit of the New Testament. Not only do they read, but they write to one another. I do not wish to take up the time of the house, but I do hope that both the house and the government will fully endorse the resolution and that we may be able in consequence to help the blind, each in his own community.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO EXTEND BENEFITS OF OLD AGE PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE.
speechtext:
I wish to go on record as heartily in support of this resolution. My association with the blind goes back a considerable number of years to the days when I was in the [Mr. Manion.J
provincial government of Alberta. A school was established in Manitoba for the education of blind persons, and from that time on no one who has come in contact with the blind there can have helped being struck by the fact that something should be done in a public way for people so afflicted. Of course, we must not lose sight of the fact that there are a great many blind people who make a success of their vocations. I have in mind one or two who have succeeded. I know of a young man who became blind during his university career, and he is making a splendid success to-day in the field of insurance, as a solicitor, so that he is able to support himself and his family. In the main however this affliction is a severe handicap to numbers of people throughout the country. No later than last session I was one of those in the House of Commons who pleaded for more consideration by way of grants to the associations that were looking after the interests of blind persons.
I have nothing to add to what was in my opinion very ably put yesterday by the mover of the resolution, except to say that I wish to go on record as being heartily in accord with the idea of parliament taking this matter up and doing something tangible for those unfortunates in our country who are stricken with blindness.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO EXTEND BENEFITS OF OLD AGE PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE.
speechtext:
I desire merely to record my approval of the resolution before the house. I can imagine no resolution calling for legislation that will appeal to this house in a greater degree than the one moved by the hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. Cotnam).
The point has been made by the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) that some persons afflicted with blindness have made a success in life so far as monetary independence is concerned. That of course is true. An outstanding case is probably that of Sir Charles Lindsay who recently received knighthood for his benevolent and charitable work and who has been able by his industry to acquire very substantial wealth. But the proposal of the resolution, as I understand it, is to extend the Old Age Pensions Act to those afflicted with blindness so that they may come under its provisions at the age of forty years. Blind persons who are deprived of sight to view the glories of creation appeal in a special degree to our sympathy and support, but over and above what charity and institutions have done to alleviate the afflictions of those who have never seen the light of day or the glory of the sun, over and above those

Pensiom for the Blind
who are aided in this way there is still a large class of blind people who require assistance from the state and no class of people can more strongly or reasonably look to the state for aid than can the blind.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO EXTEND BENEFITS OF OLD AGE PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE.
speechtext:
I would like to add just a few words to what has been said respecting the resolution of the hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. Cot-nam). In the border cities we have a considerable number of blind and every year a delegation waits on me asking me to use my endeavours to assist them by way of a pension as outlined in the hon. member's resolution.
While I am on my feet I wish to say that since the war the Lion's Club, one of the service clubs of Windsor, has been doing yeoman work for the blind, that is in establishing them in vocations that they can carry on and also assisting them financially. If it were not for that organization, the blind would be in a much worse position than they are in to-day. I believe these matters should be drawn to the attention of the house when service clubs are doing such good work on behalf of the country.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO EXTEND BENEFITS OF OLD AGE PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE.
speechtext: I am very glad to observe the unanimity with which the house has received the resolution of the hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. Cotnam). Under the circumstanoes it will be extremely difficult for the government not to afford some relief to the blind in accordance with the suggestions contained in the resolution now before the house. I understand during this session the government will bring down amendments to the Old Age Pensions Act and my own suggestion would be that the government should incorporate in that act the essence of the resolution under discussion. The blind themselves have for a number of years agitated for a pension at the age of probably twenty-five years and over and I sincerely hope the government will follow the lead given in other countries by other governments and give this unfortunate section of our community that pension which we all agree they ought to have. The expense involved is very small in comparison with the results achieved.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO EXTEND BENEFITS OF OLD AGE PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE.
speechtext:
The resolution before the house needs very little explanation. I am sure every hon. member will readily recognize the necessity for a movement of this nature. These blind people in many instances are protected and provided for by their parents but when they arrive at the age of forty, ofttimes they are destitute
and a consideration of this sort would be a kindly gesture on behalf of those who have been bereft of their sight.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO EXTEND BENEFITS OF OLD AGE PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE.
speechtext: I wish to compliment the hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. Cotnam) upon bringing up this resolution. He made a very valuable contribution to the literature of the subject in his introduction of it. Blindness in the great majority of cases comes on through no fault of the individual so afflicted. It may come on as a result of accident, nerve disease or as a consequence of infection during a very early age. There are special reasons why blind people should receive help from the state. Probably the first one is that they are unable to compete in the labour market and make a living for themselves; second, by the very nature of their affliction they require extra help, attendance and services and we all know the friends and relatives are often unable to assume the burden of caring for those blind people. I therefore will give the resolution my hearty support.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO EXTEND BENEFITS OF OLD AGE PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the observations made by the hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. Cotnam) yesterday on this resolution. No one could fail to be impressed by the picture he spread upon the record with respect to those who suffer the great affliction of blindness. There are, of course, and have been for centuries, societies and individuals that have carried on beneficent activities for the relief of those who suffer from blindness. In this country votes of money have been made by the dominion government, and I believe by perhaps all the provincial governments, towards the assistance of such societies and others engaged in helping those who suffer from this great affliction. The hon. member for North Renfrew has for many years given a great deal of thought and study to the subject matter of this resolution.
The resolution suggests that the Old Age Pensions Act should be amended to apply to blind people over forty years of age. As the mover explained, the age of forty years was adopted perhaps arbitrarily, but he suggested, and I think his reasoning was sound, that if an earlier age were fixed it might in some cases act as a deterrent to blind people taking advantage of such opportunities as are theirs to become self-supporting. That might occur in some cases, but I doubt whether it would in the majority of cases. Personally I do not think an amendment to the Old Age Pensions Act would be the most satisfactory method of dealing with a question of this character. The Old Age Pensions Act is legislation of which some provinces avail themselves, others do not. If this resolution results in legislation it might well take the form of a special act, dissociated from old age pensions.
The question of cost has always to be considered in matters of this kind, so I think that feature should be made manifest in order that the house may thoroughly understand what they are embarking upon if legislation is introduced following this resolution. I am sure every member of this chamber agrees with me that we should do everything humanly possible to alleviate the lot of those affected with blindness. This house has been in years past and is presently engaged in many researches in order to help those who by reason of this misfortune cannot help themselves. If there is a class to whom we might well devote some time and some money it is that class to which this resolution relates.
I think the only committee that could deal with the matter would be the standing com-

mittee on industrial and international relations-and I would ask the hon. gentleman who introduced the resolution to move that it be referred to that committee in order that they may take it into consideration from the angles I have suggested and others, because it is an important matter. I believe the purpose would best be served in that way. If the hon. member does not care to make the motion I would undertake to move that the resolution be referred to the standing committee on industrial relations.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO EXTEND BENEFITS OF OLD AGE PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE.
speechtext: Before the hon. member closes I would like to say a word in support of this motion. I think the object of it is good, but it should not be confined to the class entitled to claim old age pensions. In the province from which I come, in which I am more familiar with the existing state of affairs, we have some very deserving institutes, the Montreal Institute for the Blind, the Nazareth Institute and other institutes that are also deserving of support. They have been looking after the blind for many years, or generations. I do not think they receive much assistance from the federal treasury, although they receive a certain amount from the provincial government. When the committee take up this question I suggest that it should not be limited to one class but that they look into the matter thoroughly, because if there is a class of people entitled to sympathy and wholehearted support it is certainly those who are deprived of their sight.

I do not propose now to discuss the subject matter any further, but only to say that while I am quite ready to acquiesce in the suggestion of the Minister of Labour that the resolution be referred to the committee on industrial relations for further consideration, I would like it to be with the understanding that if at all possible the matter in some form be resubmitted to this house during .the present session, in order that the blind may receive financial assistance in the near future.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ADOPTION OP POLICY IN COOPERATION WITH THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
Mr
Speaker, in regard to this question of health I do not think we should encourage the duplication of services which we have had in the past, with both the provinces and the federal government taking part. As a result there have been many points at which the work has not been done properly. I think the desire of the federal government should be made known and the work carried on under the provincial governments; I think the provincial ministers of health are quite competent to carry out the work but that it is the duty of this house to outline the course we wish pursued, since we make some grants towards the cost of the work.
One of the branches which, in my opinion, should be considered, is the hospitalization of tubercular patients. In Ontario I believe the poor people and the rich people are well looked after, but there is the middle class who are not able to pay the cost of hospitalization. So we find contagion spreading all the time. We find homes in which there may be tuberculous persons living with children, and conditions of that kind, and I believe that if something could be done to bring about more complete hospitalization of tubercular patients it would mean a great deal to the county in which I live.
In connection with maternity work the situation in Ontario is perhaps different from that of the western provinces. In the west, where the farms are far apart, hospitalization is required in maternity cases, but that is not so in the rural sections of Ontario. I have the statistics in regard to Ontario with the exception of those for the last two or three years. We had an excellent man in Ontario, Doctor McCullough, who furnished us with the statistics so that we might know what was going on throughout the province, but for the last few years that information has not been made available. According to my information, however, the maternal death rate in the cities is two and a half times as great as the rate in the rural parts of the province. I think if the Minister of Health looks into the matter he will find this statement to be correct. So I do not think that the hospitalization of maternity cases would lower the maternal death rate in the rural parts of Ontario; I think the larger hospitals will have to show that they can do better "ork than is
being done in the rural districts before we make any change in that regard. As I say, I am not speaking of the western provinces. People on farms there are further removed from medical assistance, but in Ontario by far the best record is found in the rural districts and villages, where the family doctor practices. I have the statistics for each city and each county for a number of years back, and I think my statement can be proved quite easily.
I might say also that in Ontario, and in fact the whole of Canada, the infant mortality rate is too high. Many other countries surpass us in that regard. I believe the average in Canada is something over 89 per thousand, while in New Zealand it is only 35. Certainly we are not among the leading countries so far as low infant mortality is concerned. According to the last report I have before me the maternal mortality rate per thousand is 5-8 in Canada, while in Italy and some other countries it is only 2-7. But while our maternal mortality is much too high I must say that it is in the rural parts of Ontario, and I presume that applies to the other provinces as well, that we find the low mortality rate of only 2-7, while in the cities it is as high as 7 and 8 per thousand.

speechtext:
I do not wish to take up the time of the house at any great length, but I should like to refer briefly to the minister's statement in connection with this resolution. First of all I wish to thank and compliment him upon the stand he has taken with regard to this all important matter of health. Early in his remarks, however, he said that he thought my address painted altogether too gloomy a picture with regard to the health of the Canadian people. All I can say in reply is that the statements I made and the figures I gave were actual facts with regard to the health of our people.
I have in my hand a short report by a commission which was formed in the province of Alberta. This commission realized the serious situation with regard to health matters and considered it necessary to draft a plan which would be sufficiently comprehensive properly to look after the health of our people. I should like to take a moment to outline the important part of that plan, as follows:
1.	The regular general practitioner service of general medicine, minor surgery, obstetrics, etc.
2.	Specialized service, special diagnostic services and major surgery.	_
3.	Hospitalization and hospital facilities such as pathological laboratory services, X-ray services and so on.
Federal Health Policy

4.	Dental services.
5.	Prescribed medicines; prescribed surgical appliances, and so on.
6.	Preventive medical service for each unit.
This service would be a full time service
similar to that now available in Edmonton, Calgary and the rural health districts operating in the Red Deer and High River areas.
I mention that plan because in one of the provinces, which I am glad to say has been congratulated by the minister they have realized the tremendous necessity for something more to be done with regard to health matters than is being done at the present time. It is because they realize these remedies should be brought about, and because of the considerable cost to that province as well as to other provinces which may follow a like plan, that I ask the house to give consideration to the necessity for making greater grants and working in closer cooperation.
I was pleased to hear the figures given by the Minister of National Health (Mr. Sutherland) concerning the great improvement which has been made due to the attention given to serious ailments such as tuberculosis, diphtheria, smallpox and whooping cough, and the resulting reduction in death rates from these ailments. I was pleased to note the minister is sympathetic to the idea of full time health units. On the whole I believe this house should be congratulated upon having a Minister of National Health who so wholeheartedly has met a problem such as the present one and who has given us such hope for the future.
The minister made some observations however concerning which I should like to speak. He said that with the exception of certain rural districts we are fairly well supplied with hospitals. That may be true so far as the older parts of Canada are concerned, but the same statement would not apply to the newer parts of the dominion. So far as the western provinces are concerned I know we could do with a great many more hospitals. While enumerating the hospitals in Canada he stated that there were 59 for the treatment of mental cases. In view of that fact it seems to me we have a situation which is more serious than I had at first thought. A condition whereby we have to have no less than 59 hospitals to take care of our mental patients is certainly not complimentary to such a young country peopled with such a robust race. Something must be wrong with our people in this northern country if we have to have that many institutions to take care of our mental patients. In those provinces with which I have been more closely in touch I know there is usually a waiting list of mental cases to enter the hospital, already built.
May I congratulate the Minister of National Health upon his statement that the ministers

of health in the different provinces are to be invited to meet in Ottawa at some date in the near future. I should like to congratulate him further upon the address he gave and the hope he has given hon. members and people throughout the country who look forward to a great deal more being done, particularly in a preventive way, to guard the health of our people. I appreciate his observation that he has no objection to the resolution before the house.

speechtext:
His honour is precluded from giving his opinion. His honour can only give his judgment upon a matter that is raised, upon a point of order being taken by a member of the house as to the propriety within the rules of discussing any resolution or question that is submitted to the house for its consideration. The Speaker of the house is not an advisory tribunal to express opinions with respect to some contingency that may or may not happen. His duty is merely to administer the rules and preserve order. As to the second there is little difficulty. As to the first, the construction of the rules, there is always some difficulty.
The opinion that was given by the former Speaker is a decision that there shall not be two discussions of a given matter at the same session of parliament. That is so fundamental for the maintenance of the institution itself that one would think there could be no doubt about its soundness.
The right hon. gentleman read from the records to show that this house had distinctly arrived at conclusions with respect to every matter mentioned in the amendment of Mr. Ralston, and a division having taken place and a conclusion having been reached it was not competent again to review that matter in the same session by projecting a new discussion into the house.
But there is also another matter to be considered, and that is that it is always competent for the house to express opinions with respect to a matter that has not been debated during the session, and up to the moment there has been no debate on the question which is now up for consideration. I was reminded the other day when discussing another matter, by my friend the Minister of

Justice that just prior to the budget being delivered increasing the British preference, the then member for the city of Halifax, the retired Judge Russell, moved a motion that in the opinion of the house the British preference should be increased by, I think, about 25 per cent. Three days later the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) delivered his budget and increased the preference by 25 per cent. It was one of those motions made by arrangement for the purpose of securing an antecedent expression of opinion, and then finding that the budget itself dealt with the matter in the way I have indicated. But I do say to the right hon. gentleman that it is wholly improper to seek from the chair the expression of an opinion as to something that may be submitted; and, secondly, if there has been no point of order taken, then the debate should proceed writhout any further question. If the right hon. gentleman raises a question of order and indicates the grounds upon which he makes his point of order, we will discuss that point of order. But until that time does arrive, I submit that there is nothing before the chair to enable it to give an antecedent, shall I say, advisory opinion upon contingencies that may never arise or events that may never happen.

They are thinking of the good that has been done to Canada and to their industry by the operation of these agreements. Two years ago 16 per cent of our imports of fine leathers came from the United Kingdom, we are now getting 39 per cent from there. Let me read a letter from one of our friends in the leather industry. This is dated January 25 last.

What is the situation in regard to patent leather? Three years ago the United States shipped to the United Kingdom 18.000 hundredweight, last year 7,000 hundredweight. Canada three years ago shipped to the United Kingdom 6,000 hundredweight, last year she shipped 11,000 hundredweight, to the value of £368,422, which money came into Canada to benefit Canada generally and the leather industry in particular.
This is what the father of the gentleman just quoted says, under date of January 29. The letter has just come to my hands. I apologize for not going on with my resolution last Monday but I wanted this information:
I agree with you that the Ottawa agreements have been of the greatest possible value to Canada. Led by the premier of Canada they have operated in favour of the farmers and business generally...
The writer's view is that this is one of the greatest forward steps in the empire. The rapid growth in two or three years, in all parts, together with the understanding of each other better and finding out that what they can exchange to the advantage of both will enlarge our trade as the years pass along. The leather business has been greatly benefited, more men have been employed. The empire demand has grown for our goods. It has increased 125 per cent since the agreements have been passed. We are not looking at this from any political standpoint-
Oh, oh.

but from a business standpoint, in which every citizen should be called to see the expansion, not only in our line, but scores of other lines.
I would like to turn back for a moment to bacon and ham and try to put the picture before you of what has transpired in that industry and how it affects Canadian farmers. When these trade agreements went into effect the average price of hogs in Canada was 4 cents. In Chicago it was a good deal less than 4 cents. Canada produces 6,000,000 hogs per year. What happened inside of twelve months from the consummation of these agreements? The price went from 4 cents to 64 cents, beyond that in fact, but the average for the
year in round figures was 61 cents. In the United States the price remained stationary below 4 cents. So we have 64 cents on this side of the line and 4 cents on that side, a difference of 24 cents a pound. Six million hogs per year, produced in Canada, 24 cents per pound on a 200 pound hog, represents S5 per hog. For six million hog3 it means a total of 830,000,000. Due to these trade agreements you have put into the pockets of the Canadian farmers in that one year 830,000,000 more than they would have received had these pacts not been consummated and had the United Kingdom not seen fit to restrict her imports of bacon and ham. It did not stop there; it went from 64 cents per pound to 8 cents, in round figures, in December of 1934. If you deduct 64 from 8 you have a balance of 14 cents, which on a 200 pound hog means $3, and on a production of 6,000,000 hogs means another
818,000.000 in addition to the 830,000,000 realized within the last two years. That is all due to the action of the United Kingdom in restricting her imports, making it possible for Canada to recover a portion of that market.
But our farmers have not gone far enough. In 1932 the products of 300,000 hogs went to the United Kingdom; in 1933 the products of
600,000	hogs went to that market, and in 1934, the products of 1,000,000 hogs were sent to the United Kingdom, but under these pacts it is possible for Canada to supply a quota equal to the production from 2,500,000 hogs. So we are only about a quarter of the distance that it is possible for us to go. Even since December 31, 1934, the hog market has continued to rise. To-day it is on the basis of 84 cents, and I say to the Canadian people and the Canadian farmers that this one feature of these pacts will see to it that the Canadian hog will buy the baby a new pair of shoes.

They have made trade more difficult in this country than it was before; more difficult as between different parts of the British empire; more difficult as between different parts of the world.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity afforded to discuss the Ottawa agreements, because I remember very well just before the vote took place the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) pointing his finger along these rows and daring each and every one of us to oppose the agreements, so that if there had been anything political in it surely we would have heeded the Prime Minister and voted with him on that occasion. But we did not heed him. I felt slightly wrathy at that time, because I never had a finger pointed at me and had never been told in that way before what to do. Coming from that great land of freedom I very much resented it.
fMr. Harris.]
The last speaker (Mr. Harris) has given figures and percentages, and he has endeavoured to make it appear that since the passing of the Ottawa agreements Canada has been saved from some great catastrophe. During the time at my disposal I am going into the matter a little more closely, and I shall examine what has happened since the conference agreements were signed, and even previous to that time. I shall not go back to the years between 1921 and 1929, but I shall come to a more recent date. Let us deal with the trade of Canada just previous to the signing of the agreements in 1932, and compare the trade of that time with the figures two years later, 1934. I propose to examine carefully just what the agreements have done for the Canadian people, and more particularly for the farmers and workers in industry.
In passing may I observe that in 1930 the total trade of Canada was well over two billion dollars, but in 1933 it had dropped to about $887,000,000. If one wants to find as low a figure as that for Canadian trade he will have to go back a good many years. It is true that in 1934 trade increased a little, but would we not have been in a terrible position if it had not increased. However, even with the increase in 1934, in which year there was a total trade of $1,019,479,094, we have to go back to the year 1914 to get as low a figure even as that. May I point out that in 1914 we had a population of only a little more than 7,000,000 people, while in 1934 we have a population of well over
10,000,000 people. Despite the difference in population in those years the trade figures are about the same.
I shall now turn to the figures for grains, because I believe they are very important. First I shall give the figures showing the total value of grains of all countries. In 1930 we shipped grains valued at $232,763,740. In the year of the Ottawa conference the grains shipped were valued at $132,930,429. That, Mr. Speaker, was the year of the conference. In 1934 however, the total grains exported to all countries were valued at only $128,284,392.
That is fact number one, namely that the value of the total grains exported from Canada has dropped since the Ottawa agreements were signed and since this government came into office.
Now let us examine what happened to our shipments of these grains to Great Britain. In 1930 we shipped over 113,000,000 bushels of wheat to Great Britain, for which there was returned to this country well over $139,000,000.

Empire Trade Agreements
I ask the house to take note of these figures. In 1932, prior to the Ottawa agreements being signed, we shipped to Great Britain over
110.000.	000 bushels of wheat for which we received just over 865,000,000. In order to save time I am giving the round figures only. But please note the difference in value of those two figures.
What happened to the wheat trade?

You can make your own speech after I am through. I do not want to be discourteous, but I do not want to be interrupted. In 1934, two years afterwards, what were our exports? It will be remembered that the Prime Minister told us that it was necessary for Canada to sign these agreements if Canada was to live and expand her trade, because her trade had gone, and particularly it was held out to this country that Great Britain was our great salvation. Well, let us see if Great Britain was our salvation to the extent that some hon. members are trying to make out in this house and in the country; and, Mr. Speaker, I say again that I welcome very much this opportunity of getting down to the actual facts. In 1934 it is very true that we shipped to Great Britain 112,787,849 bushels of wheat, which was a slight increase over 1932, but a great decrease as compared with 1930. But here is the astounding fact, that for that 112,787,849 bushels of wheat shipped in 1934 we received $75,699,056, while in 1930 we received $139,000,000 for the
113.000.	000 bushels that we shipped.
I heard the hon. member for Toronto-Scarborough (Mr. Harris) in his speech talking about European countries dumping their goods in Europe. What happened in our case? It is only because we dumped our goods into the old country at less than cost price that we were able to find a market for many of them at all.
I have before me the speech of the Prime Minister when he was talking about wheat, barley and oats, and the great market there was for these products. We raise, as everyone knows, considerable barley in this country, and the province of Manitoba is, I believe, famed for its barley. In 1932 we shipped to Great Britain 8,168,571 bushels of barley. That was just previous to signing on the dotted line the agreement with Great Britain. In 1934, two years later, we shipped to Great Britain only 1,398.043 bushels of barley.
Now take oats, another valuable product of this country. In 1932 we shipped to Great Britain 6,082,621 bushels of oats. After the
conference we were going to find a great market in Great Britain for our products, but we shipped to Great Britain in 1934, two years after the conference, only 4,009,382 bushels of oats.
Now let us state the total grains, including rice; it may be news to some that we are shipping rice from this country, and I am sure it must be some consolation to our farmers. In 1932, before the conference, the total of our grains shipped to Great Britain had a value of $71,330,905. That was the total just before the conference. Two years later, in 1934, the total was only $77,600,084. That was the total value of our grains shipped to Great Britain just two years after the conference, but when you take into account the vast quantities of grains that had to be shipped to make up that amount, you will see that the remark I made a moment ago that we are dumping our goods into Great Britain was very pertinent indeed. In 1930, the low year under the Liberal administration, we shipped to Great Britain $149,138,637 worth of grains -quite a difference as compared with 1934.
Now as to rice which, as I say, we are beginning to ship to the old country. In 1932 we shipped to Great Britain $14,000 worth of rice and rice meal, and two years later we shipped $4,256 worth. I am taking all the grains as I go through the list.
Let me come next to rye. The member for Toronto-Scarborough held up a bottle in order that hon. members might see it, and we have to take his word that it contained mineral water. Well, in 1932 we shipped to Great Britain 2,116,572 bushels of rye, and in 1934 we shipped only 241,820 bushels-quite a drop, two years after the conference agreements were in effect.
I notice in reading the Prime Minister's speeches that he says "what a fine country this is for growing peas." In 1932 we shipped to Great Britain 8,685 bushels of peas, and in 1934, 7,429 bushels-a considerable drop.
I come to oatmeal, which must always ap peal to those who come from the countrj north of England which is Scotland. There was a drop in our oatmeal exports. In 1932 we shipped 65,039,500 pounds of oatmeal to Great Britain, and in 1934 we shipped only 40.373,300 pounds.
Take butter. Governments have gone out and governments have come in on this one product. All these commodities I have mentioned are products of the soil and of our farmers. In 1932 we shipped to Great Britain S6,927,000 pounds of butter. Two years later, in 1934, that had dropped to 1,858,304 pounds.

Take milk and its products,
another very important item to the farming community in this country. In 1930 we shipped milk and milk products to Great Britain to the value of $16,859,942. That had dropped in 1932 to $12,410,749. After the conference it had dropped to the low figure of $9,504,252, a very considerable drop of nearly $3,000,000 from 1932, and 87,000,000 less than the last year of Liberal administration, which was one of the low years of trade.
I well remember the Prime Minister speaking about honey; I was interested in that because I happen to be a beekeeper. He spoke about having conversations with the Hon. Howard Ferguson, and told how the old country was waiting to eat up our Canadian honey. Well, in 1932 we shipped 1,948,047 pounds and in 1934, 1,853.093. These are interesting figures in view of statements made everywhere by members on the government side that the country's trade had gone down so low that nothing could save it but the agreements; if it had not been for the agreements, we are told, the country would have been sunk, but by their finding a market in Great Britain for our agricultural and other products we were saved.
Let me mention eggs, because this is one of the few articles of the farmer the export of which has increased. I will also mention bacon and hams, and let me say that there would be something terribly wrong if no article had increased. I am not omitting any of the increases during the time at my disposal along agricultural lines. In eggs. I find that while there was a great increase in shipments to the old country, we sold our eggs

in 1932 at an average of 22J cents a dozen whereas our eggs sold last year, 1934, at about 20 cents a dozen. Take dressed poultry. That showed some increase, but if you will look carefully into the figures you will find that we shipped many pounds at a very, very low price.
Coming to bacon and hams, I well remember, when that was under discussion, the Prime Minister telling the members of -this house and the farmers that we had an unlimited market in this direction. It may be true we got some concession whereby we might send up to 280 million pounds to a free market, but let us see what advantage has been taken of that concession. In 1932 we sent 15,276,600 pounds and in 1934 it had risen to 94.559,700 pounds. But if you compare the prices of bacon and hams in the old land in 1934 and 1932 with prices obtained in 1930 you will find that the product returned a value of 13 cents a pound in 1934, 114 cents a pound in 1932 and 224 cents in 1930. Now these figures are very interesting, because after all it is what the farmer gets that counts, his returns. You can talk about percentages as much as you like, but it does not mean anything to the farmer.
Speaking of pork products I notice another article in this connection and that is dry salted pork. We lost a good deal in that market, because in 1930 we sent 4,627,400 pounds at an average price of 20 cents, which had dropped in 1932 to 1,138.900 at an average of 10 cents per pound. That was the year the Ottawa conference took place, and in 1934 it had dropped to as low as 842,100 pounds, netting us an average of 11J cents a pound

a considerable difference compared to 20 cents a pound received in 1930.
I come now to the products of our fisheries. This is of considerable interest to two sections of the country, the maritime provinces and British Columbia. Canned salmon is one of the most important of our products in British Columbia. Let us see how it has fared since the Ottawa agreements have been in operation, and during the time of this administration. In 1932 we shipped 20.517,800 pounds of canned salmon to Great Britain, and in 1934, two years later, this had dropped to 12,922,300 pounds, a difference of 8,000,000 pounds, and representing a decrease of over $1,000,000 in value. I would point out in passing that the fish products of the Atlantic coast are mostly in the form of fresh or frozen fish, and the market has been lost owing to the fact that they were unable to ship into the United States, and there is little market in the old country for fresh or frozen fish.

The total of fishery exports in 1930 was $35,697,027, and that had dropped in 1932 to $24,437,078, and in 1934 to 820,779,938, or a drop of $15,000,000 since 1930, and with the fresh fish market of the Atlantic coast producers practically lost. Of the total I will indicate what went to Great Britain, taking the two years again. In 1932 we sent to Great Britain S5,481,301, and in 1934, after the conference agreements had been adopted, it had dropped to $4,6S5,328, or a drop of nearly $1,000,000 since the Ottawa conference, being almost the same quantity as was shipped in 1930.
Another product is maple sugar, which is consumed almost entirely in the United States. Our exports in maple sugar had dropped by about 1,000.000 pounds in 1934. Now, with regard to importations-
What about lumber?

Don't worry; I do not intend to omit that. I wish I had more time, because I welcome this very much. The figures in regard to flour importations will comfort our people. In 1932 we imported 21,967 barrels of flour and since the Ottawa conference the figure has increased to 51,501. I have been endeavouring to get the importations from Great Britain, which I understand were considerably larger during the calendar year 1934.
I come now to lumber and newsprint, which are products of our forests. It may interest the house to know just how these two products are divided in value and in the number of those engaged, because it is important to have these figures before us. In the pulp and paper industry there were 26,669 persons in Canada engaged in 1933, and those are the latest figures that I can secure. There were 22,361 engaged in the lumber industry in the same year, or more persons engaged in pulp and paper than in lumber production. The value of lumber produced in Canada in the same year was $62,927,987 and the value of the pulp and paper was approximately $144,000,000, so that there is quite a comparison between the two. As a matter of fact, the exports from our forests equal 30-4 per cent of the value of all our total exports. I might point out that in the matter of exports newsprint takes second place in value and that only to wheat. Pulpwood comes third and lumber takes sixth place in comparison with wheat. The total unmanufactured wood pulp which was sent to Great Britain in 1930 amounted to SI,407,870. In 1932 that had increased just a little to SI,424,159. We were told however that after *the agreements were enacted that trade would
increase. In 1934, two years later, exports of unmanufactured wood pulp had dropped to $1,313,243. Exports of wood pulp dropped from $8,196,144 in 1932 to $4,883,318 in 1934.
As regards newsprint, it may interest the house to know that one-half of the total requirements of the United States in the manufacture of all kinds of paper comes from the Dominion of Canada. In 1930 our newsprint exports amounted to $145,610,519; this dropped in 1932 to $103,003,352 and in 1934, two years later, it dropped to $73,238,482, or a fifty per cent drop in total exports and a smaller percentage of that great total going to Great Britain.
Where was it shipped to?

As regards the total amount
of newsprint exports I gave to the house, it is principally shipped to the United States. Very little newsprint is shipped to Great Britain, and there seems to be very little market in that country for it. But newsprint and the production of paper is by far the largest part of our forest products industry, and I have endeavoured to place before the house the percentages, the total figures and also the number of men employed in both industries. Therefore, when we hear people talking about the lumber industry, they overlook the point that it is just one part. If exports of lumber from British Columbia to Great Britain have increased, I might point out that we were selling the very best lumber for less money than we could obtain for it from other countries, because the average was $17.50 when we were receiving from the United States and other lands an average of $23 for a thousand feet. So when this country is willing to give away their product, and the very best, and dump it into other countries, it is no use bragging in the house that we are doing so very well.
Let me now take the total of wood and wood products including all paper exports. In 1930 our total exports were $289,566,675; in 1932 this had dropped to $175,740,279 and in 1934, two years later, during the administration of my hon. friends opposite, it had dropped to $143,142,398.
As we are going through the whole wood item, there is another little one which is that of railroad ties. Some hon. members will ask: What market is there for ties? It is quite considerable. In 1930 we sold $1,104,835 worth of railroad ties, of which Great Britain took $340,127 worth. In 1934 only $1,153 worth was sold to Great Britain,

or practically nothing. The trade to Great Britain had dropped from 8340,127 in 1930 to $49,324 in 1932, and two years later to only $1,153.
Another important item is shingles. There is practically speaking no market in Great Britain for our cedar shingles. In 1930 our total exports of shingles amounted to $6,704,494 and in 1934 this had dropped to 83,764418.
Another matter that I wish to speak on and that has been discussed here, may be debated, if not under this heading, under some other. The other evening, when the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Spotton) was speaking, I noticed that he talked of the great immigration to this country that had taken place during the Liberal administration being left on the doorstep of the present government, and they were compelled to bear the burden of it. I also heard the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) make the same statement in the house last year. I have taken the trouble to go into the figures very carefully and am now placing the facts before the house. I would draw attention to the fact that they are taken from the records, and the years I shall quote are those of the Liberal and the Conservative administrations. The Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden assumed office in October, 1911; Mr. Mackenzie King assumed office in December, 1921. For the ten fiscal years 1911-12 to 1920-21 the total immigration wTas 1,678,316 of which number 629,464 were British. In the ten fiscal years 1921-22 to 1930-31, the total immigration was 1,217,069 of which number 491,727 were British, or a difference of 461,246 more during the Conservative administrations than during the ten years of the Liberal administration. I think those facts should be placed before the house, because I have listened a good many times to other statements being made. I have gone carefully into these figures and if they are wrong I shall be glad to correct them.
Would the hon. gentleman supply the figures for the four years of the present government and for the last four years of the former government, if he has them?

I have not the figures. I
have not the immigration figures for the last four years of the Liberal administration compared with the four years of this government, but I will tell you what I do have. We have heard a lot about Canadians who went out
[Mr. Reid.l
from this country during our administration, but the number brought back was not told. Here is a return for those four years. For the years 1926-1930 Canadians returning from the United States numbered 141,359. For the four years of the present administration the figures are 68,388. For the four years ended 1930 British subjects returning numbered 13,431, while only 4,334 Britishers returned during the four years this government have been in office.
The Minister of Labour has spoken about the type of immigrants. Let me give you one example. During the years 1912-1921, ten years, the Conservative government allowed 36,314 orientals to enter this country, consisting of 29,024 Chinese, and 7,290 Japanese. During the ten years of our administration, 1922-1931, the total number admitted was 7,141. Those living in British Columbia feel very keenly about that.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Toronto-Scarborough (Mr. Harris) one would think that not only were we returning to prosperous times but that conditions in this country were ideal. It is time someone put before this House of Commons what in my opinion is one of the most outstanding and extraordinary situations facing the Canadian people to-day. Who is going to pay the taxes? The position is this; the municipalities all over Canada are obliged to increase taxation in order to get revenues to meet their budgets, even those which are able to meet their liabilities. The provincial governments are driven to finding new sources of taxation. The federal government has got to the stage of bringing down legislation which will increase taxation considerably. Where is the money to come from to meet the increasing taxation with which we are faced at the present time?
From the empire trade agreements.
And you rescinded the treaty.

You bet we did. The government said, "Put us in power and we will put the price of butter back to 50 cents a pound." The farmers believed them and voted for them. When the next election comes along what are they going to do about the butter question? You fellows that slid in on butter will slide out in the same way.
Why did you rescind the treaty?

The duty on butter, under the King administration, was four cents per pound. That treaty was rescinded. This government did not say they would raise the duty; they said they would not allow Australian or New Zealand butter to come into this country to the detriment of the farmers of the eastern townships, and because of that promise they received many votes. Now this government has placed a duty of five cents per pound against butter coming
Empire Trade Agreements

into Canada, but what has happened? The depreciated currencies of those countries, as against the gold standard prevailing in Canada, technically speaking, has enabled them to bonus butter to the extent of five cents a pound, to the detriment of our farmers.
How did this government handle the butter situation last winter? They said to New Zealand and Australia, "If you continue to ship this butter to Canada we will have to do something to stop it." They had done nothing except impose a duty of five cents per pound. Then they said, "This is what we will do. You bring your butter to Canada and place it in bonded warehouses in British Columbia and Halifax. We will tell you when to sell it and when to stop selling it." This was under the administration of the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) and the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir). Every time butter went up to 31 cents a pound they telephoned from Ottawa to Halifax and Vancouver, saying, "Unload your butter," and that butter was sold- until our price dropped to 29 cents. Then Ottawa said, "Stop selling your butter." Then, naturally, our butter went up to 30| or 31 cents, and the government telephoned again, "Sell some more New Zealand and Australian butter," and when the price dropped below 30 cents they telephoned again and had that sale stopped. Why, Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister was in opposition I heard him abuse the previous government for the instability of their tariff policy. What do you think of what I have just cited as a tariff policy on butter?
