Mr. Speaker, a few
moments before six o'clock the Prime Minister rose to speak to a point of order and to make a correction. He did so, as he said, just to make the record complete. I hold in my hand a copy of the Sherbrooke Daily Record, an independent newspaper which most of the time has supported the government of hon. members opposite. I shall quote the exact words, as reported in this newspaper, of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) who spoke at a meeting held at Ayer's Cliff which was attended by Mr. John T. Hackett, the member for Stanstead, Doctor F. H. Picket, the member for Brome-Missisquoi, Doctor J. C. Moore, the member for Chateau-guay-Huntingdon, Mr. J. E. Tetreault, the member for Shefford, Mr. Samuel Gobeil, the member for Compton and several others. Referring to this famous agreement, or this telephone tariff policy, the Minister of Agriculture used the following words:
And to the everlasting honour of the Australian government this undertaking was adhered to in both the letter and the spirit, despite the fact that it was written in no treaty, placed in no memorandum, but merely made by word of mouth between Mr. Maloney and myself.
I leave it to the house to judge the accuracy of the Prime Minister's correction.
Let me illustrate one of the fundamental reasons why the farming industry is in the bad condition in which it finds itself to-day. This condition may be due not so much to low prices-and prices are very low-as to the unbalanced condition between the price the farmer has to pay for what he buys and the price he receives for his produce. About Christmas time I was called to the office of two young men who about that time had purchased an insurance brokerage business and were drawing up their first annual statement. While I was with them the door of their

Empire Trade Agreements
office opened and a gentleman dressed "dans l'etoffe du pays," apparently a real farmer, walked in and inquired as to the amount of his indebtedness. One of the men went to the ledger and said, "You still owe us thirteen dollars." The farmer handed over a five dollar bill and said, "If I can get you another five dollars to pay on the amount still owing will you wipe off the balance?" The insurance man replied, "Well, you must remember the fire insurance premium on your building expired some time ago and we have carried your account for almost three years." The farmer replied, "I appreciate what you have done, but do you know how I got that five dollar bill? This morning I brought to the Sherbrooke market twenty bushels of potatoes and sold them for twenty-five cents a bushel. I have brought you the five dollars to pay on my account."
Such are the conditions the farmers have to face. After that farmer had ploughed the ground, had disc-harrowed it, had fertilized it, had planted his potatoes, had chased away the potato bugs, had dug the potatoes and had delivered to the Sherbrooke market, all he could bring down in one load, he received only enough to pay about one-third of his insurance bill. The consequence is that his buildings are not insured to-day, and if they would be destroyed by fire he would lose their value.
I should like to say a word concerning beef prices and in that connection may I relate an actual incident. After I have finished hon. members will have some idea of what is happening to beef prices on that famous market into which the Prime Minister was going to blast his way. A merchant living at Wotton in the county of Wolfe had to get some money to meet his bills from the wholesaler, and with that in mind he set out on the ranges to interview farmers who owed him money. He went to a certain farmer and said to him, "I must have some money on the account you owe me. I have been reasonable in my treatment of this account, but I really must have money; how much can you pay me?" The farmer answered, "Well now, the interest has not been paid on my mortgage, my taxes are due next month, and I have no money in the house. I should like to pay you, but how can I?" The merchant, who was a fairly keen business man, asked if the farmer had something he could sell. He said, ''I will buy anything you have for sale and will be pleased to credit it to your account." They went to the barns and looked over the stock which the farmer did not want to sell but which, in order to meet 92582-24
his obligation, he let the merchant have. They finally agreed on a purchase price for two two-year-old steers, in splendid condition, two farrow cows, well fatted, and one cow still milking. After a great deal of bargaining the merchant allowed the farmer $40 for the five animals. The farmer thought the merchant was stealing them, and the merchant thought the farmer had driven a hard bargain. Next day the merchant sent a truck to the farm and had the five head loaded and taken to the Montreal market, where they were placed in the pens. The cattle were seen by different buyers, fed and watered. The truck had carried them from the farm to the market, a distance of one hundred and forty miles, for $3 per head, a reasonable charge. Finally the statement came through the mail. There was a large sheet checked off in columns showing inspection charges, watering charges, feeding charges, unloading charges, and charges of all kinds. It was shown that the cattle had weighed 2,755 pounds and that they had sold at the price of one cent per pound. The net result was that after deducting the charges, the merchant who had paid $40 for the five head received a cheque from the market for $4.79. I repeat, he received $4.79 for five head of cattle on the market of Montreal, and I have in my hand a photostatic copy of the cheque. I shall not give any names. This government has been in power almost five years, and yet a merchant who sells five head of cattle receives only $4.79. When conditions are as bad as that I say it is time to have a change of government.
Tell us the real story.

The hon. members for Compton, Brome-Missisquoi and Stanstead are taking sides with the farmers-and) rightly so. They come from rural constituencies; especially is that true of the hon. member for Brome-Missdsquoi. What have the members sitting behind the present government obtained for the farmers in their constituencies? They tried to obtain an increase in the price of fluid milk, after our market in the United States had been cut off. However this government did not take any action; it did not get an increase in the price of milk. On the contrary it did absolutely nothing to support the prices farmers in the eastern townships received for their milk. However the provincial government stepped in.
When?

About a year ago.

Empire Trade Agreements
After a committee had been organized in this house, and they were forced to it.
Why did you not take that step?
We had not the authority.

But according to the Prime Minister you have the authority to do other things you are going to try to do at this session. The price of S1.35 per hundredweight which the farmer received in Sherbrooke was raised to SI.80, and SI.85 in Montreal, with no surplus thrown back, which means an actual increase of practically fifty per cent, and all of this increase went to the farmer. This milk problem may be one for the provincial government; I shall not discuss that question. But I say here and now that the present government did not do a single thing for members in the rural constituencies by way of helping the farmers.
I want to quote an example which to my mind illustrates the situation as well as anything. When this government came into power the basic interest rate in government financing, federal, provincial and municipal, was 4J per cent. Labour at that time was receiving 40 cents an hour and the price of agricultural products, of pork, for instance, was 10 cents a pound; and mind you, in that situation this country was fairly prosperous. Interest, after all, is only the wages of money that goes to the man who has the money; then there is the wages that go to labour; and the price of agricultural products is the wages of the farmer. Well, what happened? The price of labour went down to 15 cents an hour, and for many there was no work at all, with thousands going on the unemployed list. The price of agricultural products, of pork, for instance, which I mentioned a moment ago, went down to 2J cents a pound. But what happened to the interest rate? Not only did the interest rate jump up considerably, but this banner province of Ontario, which boasts of its financial standing, put out a thirty million dollar issue of bonds at 6-15 per cent interest. Now, Mr. Speaker, if the interest rate had stayed where it was or had gone down proportionately with the wages and the price of agricultural products, the situation would not have been so bad; but when a government sits in power and allows the interest rate to go up nearly two per cent while the wages of labour are coming down from 40 to 15 cents an hour, and the price of agricultural products is coming down from 10 cents to 2J cents a pound, the government 
has to do one of two things; it has either to raise the price of labour and the price of farm products-and I say to the government, you have not been able to do that-or decrease the interest rate.
Or resign.

Not so very long ago the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) spoke in this house and suggested that interest rates be cut, and cut immediately, and he made a great plea for lower rates. The Prime Minister followed him and made this statement, which you will find in Hansard: " The hon. member suggests decreasing the interest rates. That is a sacred contract." A sacred contract! I want to ask you, Mr. Speaker, if there is any man in this house who is qualified to distinguish between those two kinds of contracts, the contract with the labouring men and the farmer, and the contract with the moneyed man, and then tell this house and the Canadian people that the contract with the moneyed man is sacred but that the contract with the labour man may be broken, that you can just throw him out on the street if you do not need him any more, and that for farm products you can pay the lowest price at which you can get them.
He had not talked with Litvinoff then.

No, perhaps he had not
discussed it with the Russians at that time. But this is a serious question, Mr. Speaker. When we realize, after all this talk about the Canadian National Railways, that there are in the hands of the public over two billion dollars in securities, including the advances the government has made, on which this country is paying five per cent interest, it is obvious that if that debt had been refunded even in 1931 we would have saved the taxpayers of this country two per cent interest on two billion dollars, which is forty million dollars a year.

When did the Canadian
National Railways owe two billion dollars to the public?
The Minister of Railways certainly is not serious when he asks that question.
I am serious.

I stated just previously
what they owed directly to the public, together with the advances which the government have made to the railway and which are carried in the national debt of Canada.

Empire Trade Agreements
So what difference does it make? The total indebtedness of the Canadian National Railways, including the money advanced to them, is in excess of two billion dollars, and the minister knows it. I repeat that if that debt had been refunded it would have made a saving of forty million dollars a year. But no, that is a sacred contract.

I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that that statement should go out to the public. The bonds owing by the Canadian National Railways are $1,255,000,000, not $2,000,000,0000, and the interest payable is on that $1,255,000,000; so refunding at two per cent less would not make a saving of $40,000,000.

Mr. Speaker, I do not
wish to lose part of my forty minutes by debating that question any further. I stated, and I state again, that with the money advanced to the Canadian National Railway- we advanced them, for example, $75,000,000, or something like that last year, and charged it up to the railway-including all those advances made by the Canadian government, the investment in the Canadian National Railways to-day is in excess of two billion dollars, and the Minister of Railways knows it.

You cannot refund what
is owing to the government.

But when the suggestion
is made that those bonds be refunded, the answer comes back:	Oh, you could not call
in those bonds because that is a sacred contract. But let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the Quebec Central Railroad in Sherbrooke closed their shop one night, a surprise closing that nobody knew anything about, and threw out on the street men who had spent their lives in the service of that company-one man with twenty-two years' service, and many men whose length of service was from fifteen to eighteen years-and they were thrown out on the street overnight while if they had been allowed to go on they would have become pensionable after a certain date. That was not a sacred contract, but with money it is a sacred contract.
I will go further. Mr. Speaker, and say that every single bond could have been refunded, and the Prime Minister and the government know how to do it. They could have gone ahead and called these bonds, if there was no other way, and there are several. They could have done W'hat we did during the war, formed patriotic committees, because I still have faith in the Canadian people and in the moneyed 92582-241
men in this country, and if you had appealed to them they would have come across and converted their bonds. Somebody gets up and says:	Oh, but what about the widows
and orphans and the small holders? But I say, Mr. Speaker, with prices as they are today, 65 cents of our money to-day will purchase as much as one dollar did in 1929, and therefore the person who is in receipt of interest would not have suffered any real reduction in purchasing power had the bonds been converted.
Furthermore, there would not have been all over this country the agitation that we see to-day and that is carried to the extreme of advocating no payment of interest whatever, the defaulting of obligations, and creating a situation such as has never been seen before in any other country of the world practically except Canada under the present government.
But to come back to the farmers, I want to underline this because I think it is quite important. Our farmers, no matter how they want to cultivate their own farms, no matter how much produce and fodder they want to raise, if they are going to produce milk from dairy herds, must purchase feed in the winter months. What has happened to the feed they have to buy? The price to the farmer of bran, shorts and middlings has increased some five dollars a ton, and I have had telephone call after telephone call to this effect: "Mr. Howard, it is true that we are getting a little more for our milk, but did you see the price of feed to-day as quoted in the paper? The price of feed is going up, which takes away any profit that we might have had." There was no way of getting medium priced feed for fattening purposes. Everybody in the farming game knows that you must have corn for fattening hogs, cattle and so forth. You bring in your corn, as we have been doing for years and must continue to do, from the Argentine and the United States, and what has happened to the corn situation? We imported, in 1931, 9.512.000 bushels; in 1932, 8,700,000; in 1933, 7,300,000; and in 1934,
5.200,000.	You may say, those are considerable imports. Yes, but most of it was made into corn flakes and other prepared foods for human consumption. The total imports for feeding purposes under the general tariff were
151,000	bushels, and under the intermediate tariff, 1,345,000. On the corn that was brought in for the farmer to feed his stock he had to pay 25 cents a bushel under the general tariff, while under the intermediate tariff the rate was 20 cents. But the manufacturer did Dot pay any duty at all.
Empire Trade Agreements

What has happened
to the barley grower of Manitoba and Saskatchewan?

There are many other
matters I should like to discuss, but I want to say one word with regard to industry, and I think it is only right that I should do so. The Prime Minister, speaking in this house on the address the other day, made some remarks with regard to a delegation, to show how terrible the situation was and how hard it was for the manufacturers to get along. He looked across the floor when he said, as reported on page 78 of Hansard:
Were we to allow that to continue and destroy Canadian industry? Does the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) believe that that should be done?
And so on. What he was pointing out was that a firm of manufacturers of running shoes, operating in the eastern townships, were meeting with competition in running shoes from Czechoslovakia. Very true; there is no question about it. But when we interrupted him he changed his subject, and do you know why? Because the Canadian manufacturer in the eastern townships making running shoes has to bring in his raw rubber just the same as the man in Czechoslovakia has to import his. But when the raw rubber comes in here what do you do with it? We find sales tax, excise tax and more taxes on our product, on linen thread and cotton, as well as on all the things that go into the manufacture of running shoes. The government taxes the products that go into the manufacture of the article. Well, you can place a tariff around the country and increase internal competition, which will mean a reduction in prices and a reduction in labour, but you will have the conditions which we have experienced during the past four years. And when you increase the cost of the manufacturer's raw product in Canada you may give him his Canadian market, but you will throw him out of the shoe business so far as competition in the markets of the world is concerned. If this country is to get back on its feet it must not only have the Canadian market, which is a wonderful market, but it must pay good wages to labour and also get into the foreign market. And this cannot be done if you increase the price of raw materials.
To sum up, I have only this to say. This government, to my mind, has instituted tariff by telephone, and has given bluff to the farmers and nothing to the workers, and

under this last bill it does nothing for unemployment, but leaves it a cost to the municipalities and the provincial governments. It has increased to manufacturers the cost of their raw products with the result that their foreign markets cannot be retained. To business it says, "You are done for now, because government control will be instituted," and to money it has said "good-bye." We have had a good deal of flag waving in this country in theory, but this afternoon for the first time we had a genuine exhibition of it in the House of Commons, using real flags. All I have to say is, we trust it will be the waving for the next election.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: I desire to make some observations with respect to the subject matter of this resolution. Hon. gentlemen who have preceded me will, I am sure, not expect me to follow them in their budget addresses which they have delivered in advance. There is one observation with respect to my genial friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) which I should like to make, and it is this. Surely he knows that of the billion and a quarter of bonds issued by the Canadian National Railway Company and guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada, the largest proportion has been domiciled and owned in the United States and it was obviously impossible that they could be called and converted.
You knew Australia had done it.

Australia's debt was domiciled either in Australia or in the United Kingdom, and the British government itself cooperated with the Australian government. I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Toronto-Scarborough (Mr. Harris) on having brought this subject matter to the attention of the House of Commons. There is no doubt about it that in 1932 when these agreements were before the house there was a very marked difference of opinion. I had hoped, however, with the passing of time, with the results which have flowed from the agreements as they have been demonstrated by the trade figures brought down from time to time by the various governmental departments and crystallized into a whole by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, that hon. gentlemen opposite who opposed these agreements, genuinely I believe, would have changed their opinion. And my view in that respect, I thought, had been confirmed by a statement which was handed to the press in November from behind the doors of the

Empire Trade Agreements
Liberal federation which met in this city at that time, in which statement the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in effect, implicitly if not in express terms, performed what I considered a great recantation.
You have a monopoly of recantation on that side.

I may be all wrong in the inference I have drawn from the statement handed out. Certainly we were not taken into his confidence explicitly, but I am satisfied that in the minds of the people of the country there has been left the impression that there has been a marked change in the attitude of the right hon. gentleman; and I venture to suggest that any hon. gentleman in this house, listening to-night and this afternoon to the statements made here by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke will be in absolute doubt as to what their opinion is regarding the subject matter of this resolution. So far as the hon. member for Sherbrooke is concerned, I could not, from any single phrase or paragraph of his address, arrive at any conclusion as to whether he was for these agreements or against them.
Watch the vote.
I have no doubt in that regard. The hon. gentleman is always regular; he will wait until his leader has made his statement and then follow suit.
I would not stress that too much.

There is no doubt that the trade of this country began to decline as long ago as 1929. When hon. gentlemen went out of power in the summer of 1930 they left this country with a declining foreign trade and an adverse balance of trade of 8100,000,000. There is no doubt about that; hon. gentlemen will not dispute it. All the reasons for this decline in trade are now after five years quite apparent; they were not so apparent then. But I understand they were twofold: first, all the great nations of the world between 1922 and 1930 had raised their tariffs against this country. Canada did not follow suit but deliberately, as a matter of public policy, announced at the time-and did so, as I recall it, with a good deal of pride-that this was the only country among the great trading nations of the world that had intentionally lowered its tariffs.
Tell that to the western provinces.
I understand that to be the case. That is the reason why this country became the dumping ground of all the other trading nations of the world. That was the situation in 1930.
Was the consumer benefited by that?	[DOT]

As i Live only a few minutes to go, perhaps the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) will be good enough to hold himself
in peace.
The hon. member put himself in the position of being asked that question.

Allow me to proceed. I do not think the Canadian consumer benefited; certainly Canadian industry and labour did not benefit by it, and I suggest that the Canadian labourer is a consumer as well as anybody else. In 1930, 1931, 1932 we were in the grip of the greatest depression the world has ever seen, and international trade, foreign trade, import trade, export trade dwindled from 100 to 33J per cent the world over, free trade or no free trade, protection or no protection. Canada suffered as did every other trading country in the world.
Then came the Ottawa agreements, and I venture to suggest to hon. members that the consummation of those agreements was the vindication of a principle for which hon. gentlemen opposite and those who preceded them in the seats of the Liberal party, and hon. gentlemen on this side of the house and those who led the fortunes of the Conservative party for forty years, had been striving, namely, the principle of mutual reciprocal trade within the empire. I believe Mr. Fielding's chief claim to fame in history-and I desire to accord to the memory of that very great gentleman that which was his due- will be the fact that he brought in the British preferential tariff. But I also believe that Mr. Fielding and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, if they had confessed what was in their inmost hearts, would have admitted that when they made that gesture for empire trade, they also held the firm belief that the government of the United Kingdom would reciprocate. But this did not occur.
They did.

They did ultimately. Why? Because the whole fiscal policy of the United Kingdom was changed after 1930 and it was not possible for any government to obtain mutual reciprocal trade within the empire before. I do not blame
Empire Trade Agreements

them for their failure. It was impossible for England, committed to free trade as she was during all that long period of years, to have admitted the principle. Mr. Chamberlain at one time would have been agreeable personally to doing it, but he simply could not bring the British people to his way of thinking. After 1930 there was a change in the fiscal policy of the United Kingdom and these agreements which all parties in this country were eager to explore and adopt came into being and ought to have been accepted as the triumph of a great principle for which Canada had stood for forty years.
There is no doubt-and we might as well face the situation fairly-that from 1929, and perhaps prior to that time, down to the spring of 1933 the trade of this country had steadily declined. Hon. gentlemen opposite will say that this was because we raised the tariffs against imports. That has been dealt with so effectively and so many times on the floor of the house that I do not propose tonight to traverse the situation even for a single moment; but I say this, that after the Ottawa agreements had been in force for a few months, after they had been in force for a full two years as they were in November, 1934, the usefulness and benefit of these agreements fully demonstrated themselves and they are to-day the bulwark of Canadian commerce. What happened? Adverse trade balances were changed into favourable ones. Exports increased. We formerly had to export gold or borrow in foreign countries to pay our indebtedness, and to-day this country closed the calendar year, if you include the export of gold as a commodity, with a favourable trade balance of a quarter of a billion dollars. Canada has maintained her place as the fifth trading nation in the world and we have per capita the largest foreign trade, I believe, of any trading country on earth-154 a head. That is something for Canada and Canadians to be proud of, as compared with S34 per capita in the United Kingdom and S14 per capita in the United States. Surely that is an enviable position for a little country like Canada.
I have with me to-night a statement of just what the trade of this country has been very recently in regard to the empire agreements,
and I desire very briefly to lay the facts before the house. During the twelve months ended November 30, 1934, domestic exports from Canada to British Empire coimtries totalled in value $334,785,000, as compared with $217,203,000 in the twelve months ended November 30, 1932. This is a gain of $117,582,000, or exactly 54-1 per cent.
In 1934 our exports to foreign countries reached a total of $308,181,000 as against $287,245,000 in 1932, a gain of $20,936,000 or seven per cent in the face of all the adverse tariffs that have been raised against this country. The gain is not as large as we would like to see it, but it ds a gain and a substantial one. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) this afternoon referred to the decline in the wheat trade. I suggest to him that the figures which I have given and will give a little later showing the character of our trade has changed. But the trade is there. No one knows it better than the hon. gentleman from British Columbia in connection with the export of lumber. If they do not know it we in eastern Canada do. In 1934 the exports to foreign countries from Canada reached a total of $308,181,000 as against 8287,245,000 in 1932, a gain of 7 per cent. Imports from empire countries in the same twelve months, ended November 30, 1934, amounted to $156,956,000 as compared with $129,332,000 for the twelve months ended November 30, 1932, an increase of over $35,000 000 or over 21 per cent. May I add that in November alone our total foreign trade was in excess of $115,000,000, or at the rate of nearly a billion and a half dollars for the year. If we keep up the rate of advance that we have established since the empire trade agreements came into full operation we shall soon be back to the two billion dollar mark for foreign trade. Surely that is an achievement of which this country and every citizen in it ought to be proud, in the face of economic conditions to-day.

Surely these figures are impressive. Surely they show that Canada is leading the way back to a substantial and healthy foreign trade. Surely they demonstrate the efficiency of the imperial conference trade agreements.
To the hon. member for Sherbrooke I would say that corn is not used altogether in making corn flakes. I am sure the statement he made in that respect was intended only as a joke.
I have been endeavouring to get an exact statement of the trade of this country for the full calendar year ended December 31, 1934. The particulars have been delivered to me in a form in which they are difficult to use, but I desire to put on record a few figures taken here and there from this statement. Dealing first with our total domestic exports to the United Kingdom, these have grown from §178,000.000 in 1932 to 3270,000,000 in 1934. The exports under this group comprise many items. I should like to advert to a few which are the products of our primary producers. In 1932 this country exported to Great Britain, 1,386,479 barrels of apples of a total value of §5,639,946. In 1933, the first year of the agreements, that export had just doubled in volume, 2,640,110 barrels with a value of §10,061,000. Surely these figures demonstrate the value of the empire trade agreements to
the apple growers of the Annapolis valley. If hon. members have any doubt of that let them ask the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley). He knew the value of these agreements to his people when they were brought down, and as was his duty he voted for the principle of them. I think he was very wise; I think he will agree with that himself. So I cannot understand the attitude of hon. gentlemen who oppose these agreements, having regard to the benefits that accrue to them in their own constituencies.
Let us take lumber. I think I know something about lumber. A man could not be born and brought up in New Brunswick and practise law and be engaged in litigation there and see the operations of the lumber business from day to day without knowing a little about lumber. I know this, that our trade in lumber with the United Kingdom for many years had dwindled to practically nothing. Then after these agreements were brought into effect a start was made in the right direction, and the growth of the trade, while it has not been phenomenal, while probably no great fortunes have been made out of it, has nevertheless been impressive. So impressive has it been that our people in that part of the country at all events are very anxious
Empire Trade Agreements

indeed to consolidate their position in the English market. They are watching very closely the effects of the proposed arrangements between the Soviet republics and the timber distributors of the United Kingdom. I want to say that the very matter in reference to which the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Hanbury) interrogated the Prime Minister this afternoon, is one which has occasioned great anxiety to the lumber producers of eastern Canada, because we desire to sell our spruce to the United Kingdom. We have had under these agreements a sheltered market for many of our products there. Our position is not quite so clear with respect to lumber, but because of the inclusion of article 21, I think it is, in the- United Kingdom-Canada trade agreement, we enjoy the privilege of appeal to the government of the United Kingdom in regard to the " fall clause " in the timber agreement with the Soviet republic. That article was included in the agreement at the insistence of this government. Up to the present it has not been necessary to make use of it, but if it should become necessary to do so that provision will be of the very greatest advantage to the timber exporters of the eastern provinces.

I was pointing out methods of comparison.
I believe I have made it clear that hon. gentlemen opposite assert that hon. members on this side of the house should not make comparisons between trade as it is to-day and as it was in the days when the Liberal party held office. However, when they come to a discussion they attempt to show that a great improvement has taken place in the last two years by making their comparisons with trade at the lowest point it has been since they held office. I think

the truer comparison, although it is not absolutely accurate, would be neither of these extremes, but the mean which lies between, namely, a comparison of present trade with trade as it was at the time hon. gentlemen came into office in 1930. In other words, if comparisons are to be made at all, that is a much fairer basis upon which to make them.
But even in making comparisons on that basis one has to consider that there are many factors which account for the trade between Great Britain being what it is to-day, factors that are apart altogether from the Ottawa agreements. There are world factors which have affected the whole course of world trade, have had their effect upon the trade between Great Britain and Canada and would have had their effect if there had been no trade agreements. May I say, however, that had there been no Ottawa agreements these world factors would have had a much more favourable effect upon the trade between Great Britain and Canada than has been the case under the trade agreements. Some of these world factors are perfectly obvious. Just to give point to what I have said, may I draw attention to the trade between this country and the United States, showing how it has increased over the same period in which trade between Great Britain and Canada has increased. .May I draw attention also to the fact that ever since the present government came into office, and indeed before, we have had a much larger volume of trade with the United States than with Great Britain. When we are discussing the operation of any agreement and its effect upon trade we have to consider the effect upon trade as a whole.
What are the facts with regard to trade between Canada and the United States as compared with trade between Canada and Great Britain since the Ottawa agreements went into effect? I do not think it will be argued by hon. gentlemen opposite that any increase of trade between Canada and the United States was due to the Ottawa agreements. The Ottawa agreements were enacted, amongst other things, to make trade with other countries as difficult in comparison as it could possibly be made. What has our trade with the United States approximated in millions of dollars, giving the figures in round numbers? For the twelve months ended October 31, 1933, our total trade with the United States was 8372,000,000. Our total trade with the United States for the twelve months ended October 31,1934, was 8492,000,000, or a gain in that one year of 8120,000,000. With the United Kingdom our total trade
for the twelve months ended October 31, 1933, was $293,000,000, and in the next twelve months, ended October 31, 1934, it was $383,000,000, or a gain of $90,000,000. In other words, after the Ottawa agreements went into effect our total gain of trade with Great Britain was 890,000,000, but our total gain of trade with the United States was
8120,000,000. I submit that nothing more than that is necessary to prove that so far as there has been an improvement of trade in this country, it is due not to the Ottawa agreements but to something else. It may well be that the reason our trade is not greater than it is with the United States, and also with Great Britain, is found in the Ottawa agreements; but certainly it cannot be claimed, in view of the figures that I have given, that the increase of trade between Canada and Great Britain is due in particular to these agreements.
Another factor that should be taken into consideration is the method by which these agreements have been administered, the method by which all our tariff legislation has been administered. We well know that for a time trade came about as nearly to being embargoed as was possible. As I have said, we got down to the flat tire phase in 1932, and then when hon. gentlemen opposite, through their endeavour to restrict trade and to develop a policy of economic nationalism for the country, had pretty nearly ruined the country altogether, they began to see the necessity of easing up on some of the restrictions they had previously imposed and of administering many of the laws very differently from what they had been doing theretofore. That of itself, which made for greater freedom of trade, in other words that step in the direction of Liberal policy, began at once to make itself felt, and as some of the restrictive measures and methods of artificial valuation and the like were made less exacting than they had been, trade naturally responded to this opportunity to flow which previously had been denied to it. I submit that if one had the time to do so, he could show that all the increase in trade that came about was due to some relaxation of the tariff barriers and restrictions which had been imposed by hon. gentlemen opposite under these agreements or under their administration of their terms.
There is another factor so far as trade between Canada and Britain is concerned: it rs what has taken place in Britain itself in regard to some of the other countries with which she trades. I shall mention only one. We all know that there has been an unfortunate difference between the Irish Free

State and Great Britain ever since these agreements went into force or shortly after. With what result? With the result that so far as cattle and some other commodities are concerned they were not shipped to the same extent from Ireland to Britain as had previously been the case, and at once there was a demand, not due to the Ottawa agreements in any sense of the word, but due to the situation that had been created between Ireland and Great Britain, whereby trade from Ireland was restricted and lessened, and greater opportunity thereby given to trade from Canada. But that was not in any way the result of the operation of the Ottawa agreements.
May I point out also that since the Ottawa agreements have come into force, our currency has very considerably depreciated. From the time hon. gentlemen opposite came into office up to the time of the Ottawa agreements our currency depreciated. When you are taking account of the figures of trade as they were in the days of the Liberal administration, it is to be remembered that our dollar was valued at one hundred cents, whereas to-day under hon. gentlemen opposite it is valued at around sixty cents. That of itself will account in very large measure for this supposed increase in trade that has taken place in the last few years, and it is something apart altogether from the Ottawa agreements. These are only a few of the things that might be mentioned. Innumerable factors enter into the matter of expansion and restriction of trade; I have mentioned only four, but I think the four are sufficiently obvious to make perfectly clear the point I have been seeking to make.
Apart altogether from statistics, the only way in which a true comparison can be made in respect of the operation of these agreements is to ask ourselves what trade would have been had there been no Ottawa agreements at all? What would trade have amounted to had the policies which were in force when the present administration came into office been continued-had a policy such as that which was laid down by the Liberal administration in the so-called Dunning budget been followed as compared with what we have as a result of the Ottawa agreements? That is the only true basis of comparison. Here may I say that we come to something that is fundamental in the Ottawa agreements, namely that the Ottawa agreements are founded on a policy of protection. They are founded on a policy of restriction of trade, not on a policy of greater freedom of trade; and in estimating how they have operated one has not merely to keep in mind the actual results (Mr. Mackenzie King.]
of the agreements as we see them, but also, as far as we can endeavour to see what the trend would have been, what in all likelihood would have been the result of the operation of the different policies which hon. gentlemen opposite changed when they came into power. Now, this last factor is not capable of being reduced to a definite term. In the nature of things we cannot say exactly that so many hundreds of thousands of dollars or hundreds of millions of dollars of difference would have occurred; but what we can readily see is how entirely different the trend would have been had different policies remained in force.
To understand the Ottawa agreements one has to go back to the first meeting of the imperial conference in London in 1930 which was attended by the right hon. the Prime Minister, and also to what was done at the first session of this parliament; because it was at that time that the Prime Minister began to lay the ground work of his policy of economic nationalism. He began by increasing duties against all countries and against Great Britain before he went to the conference, and then when he got to the conference he told the British people that there would be no preference with Canada unless it was on the basis of a preference granted, not by the lowering of existing tariffs in favour of Britain, as had been done under Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Robert Borden and every other predecessor of my right hon. friend in this country, but by the raising of tariffs against other countries. More than that, he stated that there would be no agreement entered into until Britain herself changed her fiscal policy. When therefore we endeavour to estimate the effect of these Ottawa agreements upon trade between Great Britain and Canada, We have to ask ourselves what trade would have been had Britain not become a protectionist country but had remained, as she was, a comparatively open market so far as Canada was concerned.
The Prime Minister at the conference in London told the government there that they must change their fiscal policy from one that was in the nature of freedom of trade to one in the nature of protection and restriction of trade. He advocated a ten per cent increase in tariffs and he made it quite clear that he would not negotiate agreements with Britain until that or some change was made. How was that situation viewed? It was because of the attitude of the Prime Minister of Canada that the then Secretary of State in Great Britain said that the suggestions he was making were all humbug and that they could not be entertained. The Prime Minister of Great

3S1
Empire Trade Agreements
Britain himself said, " It is impossible; we cannot do the thing we are asked to do." And Lord Passfield made perfectly clear, in a speech in the House of Lords, what was represented as the basis on which alone Canada was prepared thereafter to trade with Great Britain, namely, that the British government must change its fiscal policy. Inasmuch as the British government were unwilling to make any change at that time, the Prime Minister came back without any trade arrangement at all.
As against that position, one has to take
the position as it would have been had the attitude proposed by the Liberal party been adopted. We knew that the conference was coming in the fall of 1930. We knew that some countries were adopting policies of economic nationalism. We knew that there was necessity to seek markets with greater effort than ever where there was a possibility of obtaining or maintaining them. We therefore made a special effort to get as large an entry of our products into the British market as possible. The Dunning budget was framed on the basis, that where we were losing trade in one direction because of tariff walls being raised by other countries we should seek to gain trade or at least to maintain what we had within the British empire where we had an open market, practically as it was at that time-the largest market in the world. As I say, we cannot assert definitely what the result would have been; but anyone who stops to contemplate what it might have been will readily see that the trade between Britain and Canada would have been infinitely greater under the arrangement proposed by the Dunning budget than it is under the changes that have been made by hon. gentlemen opposite.
I need not repeat, what is well known to everyone, that trade cannot be carried on all in one direction; and once the Prime Minister of Canada practically closed the door, if not completely at any rate in part, against trade coming to Canada from Great Britain, as was done when he raised the duties against Britain, to that extent he made it more difficult for us to sell our products in the British market. And every step he has taken in dealing with trade matters has been in the direction of raising tariffs higher and higher and making trade more and more impossible, with the result that our great primary producers in this country have had very little chance to get into the British market with their goods.
The reason Sir Wilfrid Laurier adopted the policy with respect to the British preference which he did was this. He saw that trade, in
order to be carried on at all, had to flow both ways, and his desire was, not to make trade between Britain and Canada more and more difficult but to make it relatively easier by giving us an opportunity to sell what we could in the British market, by giving Britain an opportunity in our market with respect to the things desired by our own consumers and producers.
I cannot go over the whole story of his negotiations with London, but we know that after the Prime Minister came back he showed Britain, with a stronger hand than ever I presume, that his intention was to go on raising tariffs, against Britain as well as other countries because we had the whole tariff changed in considerable part and duties put up higher than ever at the next session. Then we had the conference in Ottawa.
What took place at the conference here in Ottawa is most significant. When the British delegates were meeting with delegates from other parts of the empire, the British delegation stated in the clearest language possible what they regarded as the course that should be pursued in endeavouring to work out reciprocal agreements between the different parts of the empire; and when we come to ask ourselves how these agreements have operated, how they have affected trade, we must pause and put this question to ourselves:	What would have been the position
of trade between Britain and Canada to-day and since 1932 had the proposals of the British delegation been carried out, instead of proposals which were diametrically opposite and for which the Prime Minister of Canada was himself responsible? I am not going to say in my own words what the proposals of the British delegation were; I will read what was said in this very chamber at the opening meeting of the conference. I happened to be sitting in the gallery opposite when the Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin, who was head of the British delegation, a former prime minister of Great Britain, made his address at the opening of the conference and set out the policies which he hoped, and not he alone but the British delegation as a whole, would govern with respect to trade within the empire in any agreements that might be made. Here are his words, as reported in the proceedings of the conference at Ottawa on July 21, 1932:
What then should be the first aim of this conference? It should be to clear out the channels of trade among ourselves . . . we hope that as a result of this conference we may be able, not only to maintain existing preferences, but, in addition, to find ways of increasing them. There are two ways in which increased preference can be given-either by lowering
Empire Trade Agreements

barriers among ourselves or by raising them against others. The choice between these two must be governed largely by local considerations, but subject to that, it seems to us that we should endeavour to follow the first rather than the second course. For howrever great our resources, we cannot isolate ourselves from the world. No nation or group of nations, however wealthy and populous, can maintain prosperity in a world where depression and impoverishment reign. Let us therefore aim at the lowering rather than the raising of barriers, even if we cannot fully achieve our purpose now, and let us remember that any action we take here is bound to have its reactions elsewhere. His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom therefore place before the conference as its general objective the expansion of empire trade, brought about as far as possible by the lowering of trade barriers as between the several members of the empire.
If hon. gentlemen opposite or the Prime Minister had accepted the objective as set forth by the former Prime Minister of Great Britain, every party in this country as well as every party in Great Britain would have been as one with regard to the agreements that might have been reached. There would have been no difference whatever. The reason that we on this side objected to the Ottawa agreements was that we believed Mr. Baldwin was right in what he suggested, and that the Prime Minister of Canada was wrong. We believe that because Canada did not accept the attitude proposed by Britain, to aim at bringing about preferences through the lowering of tariffs within the empire, instead of bringing about preferences by raising higher tariffs against the w'orld, the greatest mistake was made that has been made in this country at any time. That is where our difference arises with respect to the Ottawa agreements, and that difference goes right to the root of everything respecting them. That is why we have been opposed to these agreements. It is not that wre were opposed to an agreement with Britain; we have always sought to further trade with Britain even to a greater extent than with any other country. It was Sir Wilfrid Laurier who was the first to give a preference to Great Britain. The idea of a preference did not originate with hon. gentlemen opposite; it originated with a Liberal prime minister who was anxious to further the interests of his own country and of the empire at the same time. That is exactly what would have happened had the Ottawa agreements been based on policies such as are set forth. But the policies that were made to govern were those, not of greater freedom of trade but of more and more in the way of protection, more and
[Mr. Mackenzie King.l
more in the way of restriction as between the different parts of the empire and more and more in the way of restrictions than ever as against the rest of the world.
So far as these Ottawa agreements are concerned, this was not merely an effort to further a policy of economic nationalism for Canada but from the point of view of the Prime Minister it w*as economic imperialism as well. If he had his way we would have tariffs so high there would be relatively speaking no trade with any other part of the world. It is a very different matter to make your tariff arrangements within your own empire in a way which the nations of the world generally will recognize is right and proper as between members of a great commonwealth from effecting this result in a way which nations generally resent, and which causes them not to hesitate to show their resentment when it comes to their subsequent dealings with your country. That, may I again say, is the real basis of our objections to these agreements. Obviously there is a distinct line of demarcation. Let me repeat: It is not that we are opposed to an agreement with Britain; we have never at any time been opposed to agreements, but we are opposed to a wrong method of negotiation; we are opposed to wrong principles governing, and we are opposed in the negotiations to false actions-actions that are detrimental to our own trade.
What was bound to be the effect of these agreements once they were entered into on the basis insisted upon by the Prime Minister of Canada? It is well known what took place in Ottawa; it is well known that the British delegation were told pretty plainly that they, would either negotiate on his basis or there would be no negotiations at all.

It would be a surprise to me if agreements of the kind did not give some particular advantage to certain specially favoured industries, but the kind of agreements that Canada needs to-day are not those that are going to work to the benefit of a few privileged interests in one section of Canada, but those that will do justice to all classes in all parts of the country.
The first consideration in this country with respect to every agreement should be its effect upon consumers and producers. May I now pause to show how these agreements have operated with respect to consumers and producers. In this connection I had better at once make clear why, on the basis of the policies which we on this side are upholding in very definite terms, we cannot support these agreements in the terms in which they at present stand. I have said that these agreements are founded on a policy of protection, not of ordinary or moderate protection but of extraordinary, high protection. With what consequence? What has made them more restrictive than ever has been in the manner in which they have been and are administered. So we have laid down the following as our policy in matters of trade:

I shall leave the question of the effect the trade agreements have had upon negotiations with other countries, but I wish to point out that is another reason why we cannot accept the Ottawa agreements in the form in which they stand.
One of the other main objections to the agreement-and this is another fundamental objection-is that they restrict the fiscal freedom of this parliament. That is a fundamental reason for our objection to them. As long as agreements exist which deprive this House of Commons of its freedom to deal with our fiscal policy as we think best, and as the people of the country consider best, so long will any such agreements not meet the wishes and opinions of hon. gentlemen on this side of the house. Agreements can be and in the past have been drawn which leave parliament perfectly free in the matter of the alteration of the tariff. But as hon. members are well aware these Ottawa agreements peg the tariff at a certain figure, with respect to a large number of items.
When a government seeks to bind parliament for a period of years to a certain tariff it is imposing a tax over the period of time for which that agreement stands. A government so long as it is in office may if it wishes enter into a contract, and having made the contract is in duty bound to stand by it, but it cannot bind its sucessors with respect to their rights in the matter of taxation. No government worthy of being described as a British government, in the true sense, has ever attempted to do anything of the kind. On behalf of the Liberal party I have taken very strong exception to those features of the Ottawa tariff agreement, not merely to the feature which with respect to some commodities pegged the tariff at a particular height but also to the feature which bound us for a period of years to maintain certain rates of tariff. I have said that was alienating the authority and control of parliament over fiscal policy, over taxation, over tariff, and that the Liberal party would not support a principle of the kind. I do not think it was a necessary course to follow, but it has been done, and has been done in order to rivet protection on this country, whether or not a government may be returned to power by a people who have been aroused in their indignation against the excessive protection to which they have been subjected. That feature of these agreements cannot be permitted to

remain as it is if another Liberal administration comes into office. The fiscal freedom of this parliament will have to be restored, and I do not think that any British government will take exception to an attitude of the kind. I say that because the British government have admitted that such is the right of any political party with respect to agreements to which they have not been parties.
The Prime Minister said when I mentioned this subject before: "What about the agreement your government entered into with the West Indies? What about the agreement you entered into with France"? I think I pointed out that there is a great difference between an agreement which lessens taxation and lowers tariffs and one which raises both. May I point out this further fact? There is a great difference between an agreement to which all parties in the house at the time it is presented to the house for acceptance are agreed, and an agreement to which exception is taken from the moment of its introduction. There is a difference between an agreement entered into with the West Indies or w'ith France that met with no opposition from the opposition of the day, and these Ottawa agreements. All parties in the house supported the agreement with the West Indies and with France, and as such all were under an obligation to maintain them when they were in office. There may have been a discussion of features of them, but as for a division on them I do not recall any. But, at any rate, if there has been opposition to any agreement the position we take on this side is that the party that has opposed that agreement is at perfect liberty, when it comes into office, to alter that agreement if it so desires, having made its position one of record. But that is a very different position from that which hon. gentlemen opposite are taking with respect to these Ottawa agreements, it is that they must be maintained regardless altogether of the heights to which they have raised tariffs and taxation and the time for which they bind the country. I made the position of the Liberal party on that matter very clear at the time the agreements themselves were being discussed.
Here I wish to draw attention to what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said in the course of his remarks to-night, namely, that I had at a recent meeting of the National Liberal Federation completely changed my attitude with respect to the Ottawa agreements. I have changed nothing in any particular with respect to my attitude toward the Ottawa agreements from the time of their introduction and as I have presented my
opposition to them ever since. My attitude remains to-day what it was at the beginning; what I then stated in the house was the attitude which I took towards them. I know hon. gentlemen opposite have been saying all over the country: Mr. King has said that if he was returned to power he would cancel the agreements. I have said nothing of the kind.

I have never at any time, either in this House of Commons or speaking on a public platform, said that if the Liberal party came into office they would immediately cancel these agreements. I have said in this house very clearly that if we came into office there were certain features we would wish to change, and we would reserve the right to cancel the agreements if we wished. But to reserve the right to take a certain step is very different from saying that we would cancel the agreements. May I make clear exactly what I did say? -for I have the record from Hansard here. If hon. members will look at Hansard of November 7, 1932, page 963, they will find that what I said was this:
I wish to say that I think the parliament of Canada should be free at all times to alter its tariff in any respect that it desires, and that we should not bind ourselves to maintain a certain tariff rate, even if it is fixed only so as to continue a margin of preference; but subsequent parliaments or the same parliament, at subsequent sessions, should at all times be free to alter rates of duty in any and every particular.
That is the statement that I made at the time with respect to these agreements. It is the statement which I adhere to at the present time, and it is going to be the position of the Liberal party so long as I am honoured with its confidence in the matter of its leadership.
May I give another quotation which will make it perfectly clear what was in my mind at the time I was speaking, and has been in. my mind all along. It will be found at page 1019 of Hansard of November 8, 1932, and it-was apropos the statement which was made by the government at the time these agree-
Empire Trade Agreements

meats were brought in, namely, that they were ironclad agreements. We were told at the outset that we had to support them as they stood, that we could not make a change in any item. That is why we opposed them so strongly at the outset. We were asked to accept the whole of them without a change, and to do a thing that was not done in the British parliament, namely, to accept the agreements and change the tariff by those agreements before the tariff itself had first been altered after consideration by this house in committee of the whole. We took our stand very definitely. I pointed out that in Great Britain the British government dealt very differently with the House of Commons. The British government did not seek to maintain that it was the duty of an opposition that was opposed to the agreements to continue the agreements indefinitely and with- . out any change when they came into power. What the British government said emphatically was that the obligation was upon the party that made the agreement to continue it as long as it remained in office, but that a party that had opposed it had always the freedom to make any change it might wish in regard to a matter which was contrary to its principles. Here is what I said at page 1049 of Hansard of November 8, 1932:
May I say to the Prime Minister that I cannot understand why he or his colleague, the Minister of Finance, cannot be just as frank with this House of Commons as the Chancellor of Exchequer and the Financial Secretary in England were with the British House of Commons. The statement was made quite frankly in England that, so far as the government of the day in that country having been a party to the making of it they will feel themselves in honour bound to carry out the agreement. They have said, however, and have made it quite clear, that the House of Commons is free at all times to change duties if it so wishes, and that it cannot be bound legally or constitutionally to maintain any tariff or tariffs of any particular level. When the Chancellor of the Exchequer in England says that Great Britain is bound for five years only in that sense, J say the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance should declare to this house that we are bound only to the same extent as Great Britain is. This parliament is perfectly free at all times to alter any duties that it may think it advisable to alter. As I repeatedly have said, if any time we should be in office and decide that it is desirable in the interests of the country, and in accordance with the wish of the people of this country, that tariff schedules should be changed, we shall consider ourselves free as those who believe in freedom in the matter of fiscal policy, to make such changes in the tariff of this country as we may think necessary. I want to make that very clear, so that there may be no mistake about it now or at any time in the future.

That was the position that I took. I reserved to this party, should we come into office-and I was making the reservation clear at the beginning-the right to alter any feature of these agreements that we might think desirable. We were not binding ourselves to accept the agreement in the form in which it was drafted but reserved to ourselves the right to make such changes as we wished.
I want to make perfectly clear, Mr. Speaker, what I said at the meeting of the National Liberal Federation, and it indicates what I had in mind at the time I made those statements. If the Liberal administration should be returned to power in the next general election and we have to consider the matter of these tariffs, I do not propose to act towards Great Britain in the manner in which the Prime Minister of Canada acted when he came into office. I do not propose to go to any conference or to any meeting of ministers in England, or to have any ministers of the crown that may be in the cabinet of the day go to any gathering in England and threaten and bully the British people with regard to what is a matter of their concern, when I am trying to make an agreement that will be of mutual benefit to both sides of the empire. I would deal with the British government as I would expect English gentlemen would deal with Canadian ministers of the crown in matters of this kind. I would indicate that so far as these agreements are concerned there are features that are not satisfactory to the Liberal party in Canada; that we should like these objectionable features to be altered, and that we believe the agreements as they stand are not approved by the people of Canada. The fact that we would be in office would be an evidence that they were not approved, and therefore we would wish to negotiate a modification of the agreements in certain particulars. If we could get a modification of the agreements in a manner that would serve the interests of this country and be mutually beneficial, then the agreements as modified would be continued for the period for which they have been drawn. If we could not get these modifications, if we could not get the obvious changes in the agreements which we believe the Canadian people wish to have made, then we would reserve to ourselves the right to say whether we would forthwith cancel these agreements in whole or in part or whether we would allow them to run for the remainder of the time and not carry them on for a further period.
I am making no threats; I am simply indicating the position which I believe is the sound one for any administration to take.

Empire Trade Agreements
And may I say that if a Liberal administration should be returned to office one of the very first things that would be done would be to get into communication with the British government with respect to what we believe to be necessary modifications in the agreements, on the understanding that there are certain features relating to the tariff which we would wish to have changed in this country, pointing out particularly that we desire to have the fiscal freedom of this parliament maintained. And, as I have said, if as a result of the negotiations we could bring the agreements into conformity with the will and wishes of the people of the country, then, as modified, they would be continued. But if we could not effect a change of that kind then it would be time to decide what further step might be necessary with respect to them.
That is the position I have taken from the start and it is the position which I take now and shall continue to take for the time it may be necessary to speak in public further on these matters. I have every reason in making that statement to believe that the British government will welcome opportunities to modify these agreements. I believe that in all parts of the empire there is a very keen desire to have the agreements quite materially changed. Let me direct the attention of hon. members to what has appeared within the last few days in a despatch to Ottawa as the result of a visit of Premier MacDonald's son to Australia and what he said on his return. I quote from the Montreal Star of January 24 the following:
Attempt to modify Ottawa pacts seen Malcolm MacDonald back from Antipodes visit
London, January 24-(C.P. Cable).-Reports last night indicate that Malcolm MacDonald, British Under-Secretary of State, may urge modification of the intra-empire trade agreements reached at Ottawa in 1932, following a visit to Australia. Mr. MacDonald, son of the premier, returned from Australia last night following informal talks regarding the trade agreements and completion of a_ report on emigration. The only source of information, which came from competent circles, said that the under-secretary had become convinced of the necessity for changes during unofficial talks with Australian business and political leaders.
Now everyone knows how these agreements are viewed in Australia. I wonder whether hon. gentlemen have seen a petition presented recently in the House of Lords from western Australia praying to be permitted to withdraw altogether from the Australian commonwealth in consequence of the manner in which the agrarian interests of Australia have suffered from these agreements. In December last a delegation went from western Australia to Britain to present a petition to
the British parliament, and it was tabled in the House of Lords on December 18, praying for legislation by the British parliament which would restore western Australia to its former status as a separate and distinct self governing colony in the British empire. What reason did they give, among other things? Let me quote from the petition:
In consequence of the burden of the federal tariff the economic structure of western Australia has already become seriously jeopardized and with the continuance of such burden the state of Western Australia, the primary producers, and the people of that state are faced inevitably with national bankruptcy and ruin.
The only effective means whereby the people and the state of Western Australia can be relieved from the said burden, and the said wrong can be removed, is the withdrawal of the people of the state of Western Australia from the Commonwealth of Australia and the restoration of Western Australia to its former status as a separate and distinct self-governing colony in the British Empire.
I have nothing to say regarding the effect of the presentation of that petition; I merely direct attention to the effect which has been produced in Australia as a result of high tariffs which have served possibly certain protected interests but which have made the lot of the agrarian classes in that country such that they would prefer to withdraw altogether from the Australian commonwealth. And now may I ask hon. gentlemen whether they think tariff agreements that bring about that kind of sectional difference in a country help either the country or the British empire.

speechtext: The right hon. gentleman said a few moments ago that he trusted that I would direct his attention to any misstatements. May I point out that both these commissions are sitting under arrangements made originally by the right hon. gentleman.

That may be so, but they are dealing with conditions that have come about under the administration of my right hon. friend, and they are pretty emphatic in what they have to say touching these matters.
I will conclude with this word. My right hon. friend has said that there is an impression in England that has been created there against these Ottawa agreements which is affecting some of those traders who are seeking to further their business interests in London. I think he intimated that there were certain of them who were representing, or had represented that what the Liberal party had been saying about the agreements in Canada was perhaps correct, and that the British people had formed the impression that possibly after all these agreements were not so popular in Canada. May I say to my right hon. friend that the impression that has been created in Britain with regard to these agreements began first of all when Englishmen were here as delegates during the period of the negotiations. That was the first impression. But the impression that has been deepest of all has been that created by the by-elections in this country which have taken place since the agreements went into effect; and if the Ottawa agreements are to-day regarded in England as not being popular in Canada it is because the British government and the British people have recognized that every by-election that has been fought on them since the agreements went into force has resulted in a victory for those who oppose them.
Mr. J. II. MYERS (Queens):	I have
listened with more than the usual amount of interest to the discussion which has taken place to-day on this all-important resolution moved by the hon. member for Toronto-Scarborough (Mr. Harris). It is not necessary to read the resolution; it states simply that the result of the Ottawa trade agreements merits the approval of this house. The resolution might very well have gone a little further than that; it might have said that it merited the approval of the people and especially of the farmers of the Dominion of

Canada. My chief reason for taking part in this debate is the fact that while these agreements have perhaps been more beneficial to the farmers of the dominion than to anybody else, not a single farmer in this chamber has to-day been bold enough to raise his voice in defence of them. I hope however before this debate concludes that we shall hear from farmers on both sides of the house because I would at least express the hope that among hon. gentlemen opposite there are some farmers who have a proper sense of justice and can see what a benefit these agreements have been to the farming industry of Canada.
I was particularly amused to-night, more so perhaps than on previous occasions when he has spoken, at the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). His speeches always amuse me; they are in themselves so contradictory, but he excelled himself to-night in the contradictions that were contained in his address.

speechtext: Oh, oh.
