If the hon. member followed his leader's address as closely as I did, this would be very apparent to him. It was so apparent to me that I was forced to the conclusion that the leader of the opposition is in himself a huge contradiction. He went on to tell us how as a result of the Ottawa agreements trade in Canada had shrunk; that merchants, traders and business men throughout the country by reason of the changes in the tariff-and he was speaking of the Ottawa agreements-were refusing or neglecting or fearful to enter into business contracts in the ordinary business way. Further, he went on to prove what a loss the agreements had caused to the railways and shipping, the carrying trades of the dominion. This evening the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hanson) showed us, so clearly that anyone, the dullest, could understand, figures to prove the increase in trade that had taken place by reason of the Ottawa agreements between Canada and the other British dominions. The leader of the opposition, in an effort to contradict the minister, while admits ting that the figures given by the minister were quite correct-he did not attempt to deny them-quoted an elaborate table of figures to show that the trade and commerce of Canada with other countries, and particularly with the United States, had increased by leaps and bounds, especially within the last twelve months. That in itself was, to my mind, a huge contradiction.
We know now just where the leader of the opposition stands. He went over to the old

Empire Trade Agreements
country this year to try to get his ear to the ground and to find out how the people there felt regarding these agreements. If I remember rightly, from a reading of the newspapers after he returned I would gather that he was still opposed to the Ottawa agreements; that the people of the old country were opposed to them, and that he intended to carry on his opposition. Later on in the fall of the year when he met his supporters in conference in this city to talk over some organization matters and their tactics with reference to the present session of parliament, he apparently had modified his views, and I was led to believe, at least by press reports, that he was now in accord with the Ottawa trade agreements. However, I always doubted that. I remember very well the long drawn out debates on this question during the session of 1932 when we met here to ratify the agreements. I remember very well the undying, persistent opposition that these trade agreements met with at the hands of the leader of the opposition. So when I read in the newspapers that he was coming round and beginning to favour the agreements, I always had my doubts in the matter. My doubts however are completely swept away to-night. So far as I am concerned, the leader of the opposition to-night is just where he was in 1932. He is heartily opposed to the Ottawa agreements. He seems to be opposed to the farmers of this dominion being given a fair chance at all with reference to their own business.
Then he goes on to tell us what the Liberal party will do when, as he says, it is returned to power, which heaven forbid! I have my doubts whether the intelligent electorate of Canada will again place their business affairs in the hands of the leader of the opposition. But he waxes very eloquent when he says with reference to these agreements: "When we are returned to power we will reserve the right to change, modify or, if we see fit, to cancel the Ottawa agreements." If by any chance the leader of the opposition should succeed in coming back to power he would not need to reserve the right to do anything with reference to these or any other agreements; the majority that he would then have in parliament would give him the right without any reservations whatever.
The leader of the opposition also referred to something else. He was speaking, I think, in connection with the dissension that is now apparent between the two sections of Australia. Well, I have read a good deal about that and so far as I have been able to gather I have never understood that the desire on the part
of western Australia to draw away from the rest of the Australian commonwealth had anything to do with the Ottawa trade agreements, or, in fact, with the fiscal policy of Australia. As I have read, it is purely a matter of distance between the two sections of Australia, which are very widely separated. Of course the Prime Minister checked him up on that and he dropped it quickly. Then the hon. gentleman went on to speak of some dissensions that were now taking place in Canada. He mentioned a royal commission that is sitting to adjudicate upon or to try to harmonize the differences existing between the maritime provinces and the dominion. Let me say that that commission is necessitated by reason of the fact that the leader of the opposition failed miserably when his party was in power to implement the findings of the Duncan commission appointed by them to settle the differences between the maritime provinces and the rest of the dominion. We in the maritime provinces had to wait nine years, until the Conservative party came into power, before we succeeded in getting our rights in this regard. The present government and the present Prime Minister gave us this royal commission to settle these claims.
Now as a farmer-and I assume I have as much right to speak from the standpoint of a farmer as any other hon. member in this chamber; my right in that regard has never been challenged-let me say a word with reference to the British preference. The British preference is an old question in Canada. I believe it was first put on the statute books by Sir Wilfrid Laurier's government many years ago. It is possible that Sir Wilfrid Laurier had a different idea regarding the British preference from that which obtained later. As a farmer I have given a good deal of thought and study to this question. I do not believe that there is a man in this chamber to-night who holds stronger views with reference to Great Britain and the ties that bind Canada to the British empire than I do. I am a Britisher first, last and always. Yet I like fair play even from my friends. To my mind the situation is this; under the British preference British manufacturers were allowed to send manufactured goods into Canada. I was very glad to welcome that; I would say nothing against it. But when we sought to send the products of Canadian farms into Great Britain, what preference did we get? Absolutely none. It is true that our butter and eggs, bacon and beef, entered the British market free, but so did similar products from Denmark, Holland and other European countries. And these countries were
Empire Trade Agreements

hundreds of miles distant from the markets of Great Britain but we were thousands of miles. So we were handicapped by freight rates, a handicap that we could not overcome, to-day when we enjoy a preference of ten per cent on these products entering the British market we are still only about on a par with the other countries to which I have referred, when transportation charges are taken into consideration. Let me tell the leader of the opposition that if he should come back into power and should attempt to do away with the ten per cent preference that the farmers of Canada now enjoy, he would meet with the resentment and opposition of the farmers of Canada.
Speaking of trade agreements, I do not know whether hon. members on the other side are frightened of the word "reciprocity." I am not, and I do not know why the Liberal party should be.

When the electors finally
were offered the reciprocity pact of 1911 it was by the Liberal electors that that treaty was defeated. Let us take into consideration the question of trade agreements with the United States. I shall welcome any good, sensible trade agreement with the United States, absolutely. But at the same time I can see great difficulties. It is true that in June last the president of the United States was given power by congress to negotiate agreements with other countries, Canada included, but so far as I can understand the thought and sentiment with reference to trade matters in the United States they have not undergone any change of heart. The farmer in the United States is just as jealous of a home market for his own farm products as he was in 1930 when the Hawley-Smoot tariff was put into effect to protect him. We

must be fair about these things; we cannot blame the United States farmers for that. It is the duty of the American government to protect the American farmer. It is the duty of this government, so far as it reasonably can, to protect the Canadian farmer. And why not? I have often heard the statement made that the United States is our natural market. I believe if I were to ask anyone here to-night why the United States is our natural market the only reply would be, because it is our nearest market. Let us examine that for a moment. At home on my farm there is just a line fence separating me from my neighbours on each side. They are my nearest market. But what is the use of trying to sell a horse to my neighbour on one side if he already has as many horses as he needs? What is the use of trying to sell a cow to my neighbour on the other side if he has cattle of his own to dispose of? That is pretty much the situation that obtains between Canada and the United States. Can any hon. member name anything that we produce on Canadian farms that is not produced equally well and often in greater volume on the farms of the United States? You can go on down the line and include live stock, field crops or anything you care to mention. There is one exception, however, and perhaps I may be pardoned for naming it. In the province of Prince Edward Island we grow turnips that are not equalled in any other country of the world; that goes without saying. With that exception, however, the farmers of the United States produce practically every crop that we produce in Canada, and in addition they produce several crops which I could mention that are not produced in Canada at all. Com was mentioned to-night, and let me tell my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) that it is not necessary to feed corn to hogs. I have fed a great many hogs in my lifetime, and I never fed them corn. I see no valid reason why we should allow United States corn to come on the markets of Canada in any great volume, in order to displace feeds grown here that are just as good. Our own Canadian barley and oats are just as good as corn. Someone says they are better, and that is a fact. I suppose the hon. member for Sherbrooke is hardly aware of the fact that the Canadian hog makes much superior bacon than the United States hog, which is always referred to as the soft, flabby, corn-fed hog.
I was saying that in addition to producing all the crops that are produced in Canada the farmers of the United States produce other

Select Standing Committees
crops that are not grown here at all. Only a limited quantity of corn is grown in Canada, chiefly for ensilage purposes, while corn is one of the major crops of the United States. Cotton is not grown in Canada at all, but it is the chief crop of the southern United States. In any trade agreement that may be made between Canada and the United States there should be a swap-off. It is true that they require certain commodities at certain seasons of the year, and certain other commodities at all times, that are produced in Canada, but on the other hand there are certain things which we require from them, . even among farm products. In connection with these commodities we might have a reciprocal agreement which would work to the advantage of both nations. A matter of that kind must be worked out in a sensible, logical, levelheaded way, rather than as the former government tried to work it out. After years of quietly hushing things up, with the fear that they might offend the United States; after coaxing for years for the opportunity of getting into that market, which did not want and did not need our products, they turned around and threw a brick through the parlour window of the White House at Washington. On that brick was a label called the Dunning budget, which said, "We will build a tariff wall brick for brick with your wall against commodities of a kind produced in Canada coming into this country." That was not a sensible way in which to go about such a matter; there is a much better way.
It is almost eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker. A great deal more might be said along this line, but as a farmer I just wish to add my voice to what has been said already in support of the Ottawa agreements. Let me assure my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition that if during the next election campaign he tries to lay unholy hands on the first real trade agreements to give protection to the Canadian farmers, he will meet with undying opposition on the part of those farmers.
In conclusion let me say, Mr. Speaker, that as a farmer I appreciate what the Prime Minister has done for the farmers of Canada in bringing about these trade agreements with the mother country.
